common_name: Blue Glitter Sea Holly (Electric Blue Fine-Textured Eryngium)

planting.note: Transplant divisions or started plants in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; Blue Glitter bears finely branched stems covered in small, intensely electric-blue flower heads and bracts.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, even sandy or rocky soil in full sun; rich or consistently moist soil produces weak, floppy growth in this drought-loving perennial. Blue Glitter bears finely branched, wiry stems studded with an unusually large number of small, intensely metallic electric-blue flower heads and spiny bracts, giving a more airy, glittering effect than larger-flowered sea holly cultivars. The whole plant develops a silvery-blue cast that pairs beautifully with ornamental grasses and other xeric perennials. Established plants develop a long taproot, making them extremely drought-tolerant once settled but resentful of transplanting, so choose a permanent site. Bees and butterflies are drawn heavily to the flowers, and the dried flower heads hold their color well in cut arrangements.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Veitch's Blue Globe Thistle (Classic Deep Blue Echinops)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or spring in very well-drained, poor to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Veitch's Blue is a classic selection with deeper blue flower color than the straight species.

directions: Direct sow in poor, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Veitch's Blue is a long-cultivated globe thistle selection prized for deeper, more saturated steel-blue flower spheres than the straight species, held on branching, silvery-white stems above deeply lobed, thistle-like leaves from midsummer into fall. It is an exceptional bee and butterfly magnet, particularly for bumblebees, and cut stems dry well for arrangements when harvested at three-quarter bloom and hung upside down. Plants are drought-tolerant and long-lived in poor, dry soils but decline quickly in heavy, wet clay. Divide or transplant only in early spring before the deep taproot becomes established, since mature plants resent disturbance.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Taplow Blue Globe Thistle (Large-Flowered Steel-Blue Echinops)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or spring in very well-drained, poor to average, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Taplow Blue bears larger flower heads than Veitch's Blue on a taller plant.

directions: Direct sow in poor, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Taplow Blue is a classic globe thistle selection bearing larger, more substantial steel-blue flower spheres than other Echinops ritro cultivars, on a taller plant well suited to the middle or back of a sunny, dry border. The bold, spherical flower heads and silvery, deeply lobed foliage provide strong architectural contrast to softer-textured perennials, and bumblebees and other pollinators visit the flowers heavily through midsummer into fall. Cut stems at three-quarter bloom stage and hang upside down for long-lasting dried arrangements. Plants are drought-tolerant and long-lived in lean, dry soils but decline in heavy, wet clay, and resent transplanting once their deep taproot is established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
